snippet.textDisplay: Can you do a video on how to handle things when both husband and wife have dementia? My mother and father both have it and tend to trigger each other. I live in another state so I haven't been there to witness much of this. I got an eye opener when I called them a few days ago and they got in a huge argument while I was on the phone with them. I spoke to my sister who is their primary care giver and she let me know how bad it has gotten. My sister is a full-time nurse and so is only able to check in on them, otherwise it is pretty much just the two of them 24/7. To complicate matters, my dad is practically blind and also has COPD and has been very sick and unable to breathe so that is probably why things are so much worse right now. They are not yet at the stage where they don't recognize loved ones, but the way they keep triggering each other I can't help but wonder if it is not far off. My sister is monitoring as best as she can and has already let them know that it will probably get to the point where they have to be separated. They have been together for over 50 years so we hate to do this to them. My sister is finally getting the support of our other sister and other family who live close by. For a long time they didn't believe that there was a problem. But my sister has taken mom for all the tests to verify that it is indeed dementia. Dad will barely leave the house so she hasn't even tried to get him tested. Sorry this is so long winded. I am still processing that this is all happening. I wish I could be there to help and support my sister and to spend time with my parents. I also don't feel like I can tell my sister how to handle the situation because, again, I'm not there and I haven't been there to witness all of this developing.

snippet.textDisplay: It’s time for care home when they start becoming abusive-also, if he does hit you, (or it just gets crazy) call the cops so you can start a record. Ask for a report number. Every time services have to come for whatever reason, get a number of the report. If he goes to the hospital, he’ll probably be nasty to the staff. Make sure they add that to their notes. My mother was NOT a “nice old lady with dementia”. She was a MEAN old lady with dementia. (She was also a mean young lady). I was literally afraid to be alone with her. The abuse was unlivable. She had delusions, and it was always  something was being done to her. Fury! At me. Voices coming from the tv, messages. We’re doing something to her! Slitted eyes, spitting out words. Trying to ram me with her walker. It was literally a living hell. I called it Hell House. And it was MY house! She was just mobile enough to follow me around the house, but not enough so she didn’t need help with DL. She also weighed 230 lbs, so….im 65 myself! Nobody seems to talk about what to do when your whoever is getting out of control. I did all these things for her before she started getting so vicious, and those did work, to a point but….

snippet.textDisplay: I think in terms of chronological ages and stages. If you have had or worked around preschoolers, you will recall how you spoke to, reasoned with and managed their behaviors. Modify your conversations and expectations accordingly. Too many choices create confusion. Long explanations mean nothing. Simple one or two words are often enough. Maintain a routine. Schedule naps. Have your person ‘help with’ simple tasks like folding clothes, putting silverware away, vacuuming, brushing the dog, watering plants, etc. Give one-step directions.

snippet.textDisplay:
Ahh, Jojo, without realizing it, you're asking quite the controversial question. 😅 Neuroplasticity allows the brain to reorganize itself whereby the healthier parts of the brain compensate for the damaged areas.

However, in dementia, this compensation has limits. Early in the illness (eg mild) we can see some compensatory strategies assist. Most dementias are progressive though, meaning that over time the very brain regions doing the compensating (the healthy parts) are also affected by the disease. As a result, the brain cannot fully reorganize or permanently take over ALL the functions that are being lost.

My 78 year old mother seems to not only forgetting things, she is making up entire scenarios, mostly negative to the closest people to her. So to those that don’t realize that she’s losing her mind, they “think” that she’s being abused by the people closest to her who are taking very good care of her. Luckily most stories are so fantastic that and even impossible that we can prove that what she said, never happened.
She had very low B12 so she had shots to boost it, plus she’s been taking B12 tables daily, and 5000 units of Vitamin D and some, not all of her reasoning and memory skills have come back, but.. I’ve notice that she can now remember my phone number, she hasn’t made up very many stories lately, so I’m thinking that these simple things can help. It’s likely temporary.. but it does help.

snippet.textDisplay: That happened to my brother after his stroke. When he was sitting (we had one of those chairs that raises someone up and down, plus his wheelchair) we used a "seatbelt." Once he was bedridden I believe Mom just kept the safety rails up all the time, since he didn't have the coordination to put them down, let alone get past them. If your husband can get past it, maybe put a pool noodle along the top rail (different memories sparked) or if it was me I would be considering a "seatbelt." I am not saying you have to strap him completely to the bed; what I am thinking is perhaps some kind of strap that goes around his waist and both ends attach at rails of the bed closest to the wall...like a tether, I guess. This gives him maximum movement/comfort without making him feel like he's tied down. Make sure it is soft and arranged in a way to not rub & cause sores. We do what we have to in order to provide maximum independence while still making them safe. And no, they don't always like it!

snippet.textDisplay:
BUT...does not the calm observation that a 'protested' present, one that 'isn't' supported by the past, point out to what 'remains' of a person's reason (at least in the early stages) that, as is the case with everyone, our memory is less reliable than we hope, especially in age? Is it not dangerous that they are not encouraged to still function in accordance and compliance with at least some scepticism and personal reflection if they can, especially as they hope to be somewhat independent? Delusionals of all stripes have tried to navigate a magerial world with disconnected ideological foundations and failed.

When finally a delusional gives up or loses that independence it doesn't matter, because they can be protected from their poor interface with the material world by isolating them from it. Its those who are just come on the cusp of delusion that are a risk to themselves. When we lose the rational ability to doubt ourselves we put ourselves at risk, and 'that' is the real tragedy that the dementia-delusional suffers: a complete innability to entertain a contiguously, continously materially, factually and evidenced based reality. You can't function 'independently and safely in a world when you give 'ideas' more value than reality.

But is true that you can't 'reason' with a delusional, BUT...neither can you reinforce their delusion. Its a rock and a hard place. This video would be better if it didn't try to be all things to all people. No dementia patient could manage its convolutions, so there is no point trying to pander to them. It would be shorter, and ironically more dementia complaint, if you didnt' treat the 'Care-givers' who are likely to watch it like they too were dementia patients. Stop constantly referring to yourself as Dr. Sinclair, and viewers as Care-givers. Forget the honorfic pronouns. They flatter no one. 'Info' videos needn't flatter and entertain, just convey facts.

snippet.textDisplay:
BKelly- correct! You're noticing the more you use logic and reason, the more she doubles down and pushes back. People with dementia lose the ability to reason, compare timelines, and reality-check memories, so you just end up in a vicious cycle of arguing with her.

Instead of correction, I teach caregivers to lead with connection. It means shifting the focus away from whether it’s true and toward what the memory represents.

An example of connection could be:
“It sounds like that place feels really familiar to you.”
“What do you like most about the cabin?”
“What’s your favorite thing we do when we’re here together?”

This is how to join via connection/emotionally, not factually.

Thank you for being so open about what you’re dealing with. This is incredibly common, incredibly hard, and I really appreciate you being part of this community learning a new way! Keep practicing!!

snippet.textDisplay: I retired because my husband was diagnosed with early stage dementia and Parkinson's. I am overwhelmed!!! Recently we went out on an outing with our 1 year old granddaughter. My husband got dizzy and said nothing until I saw him stagger. I told him he put all of us danger by not saying nothing. I have decided no more outing with grandkids. I am just mad-- this is not my personality.
